title: The Impossible Act: Structural Incompatibilities Within EU Law
description:
The EU AI regulatory framework is structurally incoherent. It imposes obligations on AI providers that are incompatible with foundational principles of EU copyright, consumer protection, and fundamental rights law. Under settled jurisprudence (CJEU Infopaq, 2009), copyright arises at the moment a human-originated expression is fixed — including digital outputs generated through prompts. Yet leading providers such as Microsoft, via Azure OpenAI Service, routinely generate, store, and suppress such outputs based on opaque content filters after creation, denying users access to their own works. These acts constitute unauthorized interference with economic and moral rights under Directive 2001/29/EC, infringe freedom of expression (Article 11, Charter), and violate consumer expectations under Directive 2019/770.


Worse still, user accounts may be silently flagged and restricted through automated moderation systems without transparency, explanation, or recourse, breaching GDPR (Article 22), the Digital Services Act, and the right to an effective remedy (Article 47, Charter). The AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) deepens this contradiction: it mandates infringement-minimization, yet simultaneously requires providers to engage in actions that themselves infringe copyright and other rights.


This paper argues that EU law currently forces AI providers into an impossible legal trilemma: violate copyright, breach consumer law, or suppress fundamental rights. These contradictions are not theoretical — they are already playing out in practice, as demonstrated by Microsoft’s own court filings (Microsoft Corp. v. Yadegarnia, et al., Civil Action No. 1:24-cv-2323). The result is a form of covert, extra-legal content control that undermines both the rule of law and the very notion of authorship in the digital age.
